name: Greenish Yellow
lede: Greenish yellow is a yellow tipped toward green, a color that Europeans have long found hard to like and that mineralogists, dyers and pigment makers have each had to name.

sections.title: A modifier, not a story
sections.body:
Greenish yellow is a description rather than a borrowed name: a basic color word, [[yellow]], pushed toward a second one, [[green]]. No flower, dye or town gave it its name. The swatch here is the 1955 ISCC-NBS block called "moderate greenish yellow", which also matches plate V of Ridgway's 1912 color atlas [1].

Other collections put very different colors under the same words. A neon acid yellow-green from the xkcd survey, a brownish olive from the RAL system and a second xkcd entry all sit under this name, and the four swatches are up to 20 units of ΔE apart [1]. The name is stable; the color is not.

sections.title: Rome and the yellow nobody liked
sections.body:
Latin had a rare adjective, *galbinus*, used by Petronius, Martial and Juvenal for a shade between pale yellow and greenish yellow, and always with a sneer [2]. Martial even speaks of *galbinos mores*, literally "yellow morals" [2]. Translators and dictionary authors usually render the word as "greenish yellow" [3].

Pastoureau doubts that translation. He argues that *galbinus* names a yellow disagreeable to the eye, probably from the Germanic *gelb*, and that "yellow in the German manner" would be closer, since Roman writers sneered at the yellows that "barbarian" dyers used in place of saffron [3]. The books therefore disagree on whether Rome had a plain word for this color at all [2][3]. Greek had *chloros*, listed among its yellow terms next to *okros* (ocher yellow) and *chrysos* (golden yellow) [3]. In first-century Rome, at least, the shades from orange yellow to greenish yellow were felt to belong to one yellow family rather than standing apart [2].

sections.title: Werner and the modifier system
sections.body: The modern habit of writing "greenish yellow" comes from mineralogy. In 1774 Abraham Gottlob Werner listed eight principal colors, among them black, blue, green, yellow and brown, and qualified them with modifiers such as bluish black or greenish yellow [4]. Each could be further graded as pale, light, clear or dark, which stretched his 54 colors toward 216 variants [4]. Greenish-yellow sits among the yellows in the lists Baty tabulates from Werner and the authors who followed him, between orange-yellow and whitish-yellow [4][5].

sections.title: Pigments and dyes
sections.body:
Many pigments are described as greenish yellow, but few are named for it. Orpiment, an arsenic sulfide with 60 per cent arsenic, runs from yellow to greenish yellow [6]. Barium chromate, listed by the Colour Index in 1971 as Pigment Yellow 31, is a "dull, greenish yellow" [7]. By Buxbaum's 1998 account, bismuth vanadate has been growing in popularity as a greenish yellow that can replace lead chromate and cadmium sulfide pigments [8]. The mineral bindheimite varies from yellow to greenish yellow or brown, but it was never used as a pigment in its own right [9].

Among synthetic colors, the disazo condensation yellows, first made by Ciba in the early 1950s, range from greenish yellow to orange [10]. The nineteenth-century yellow lakes known as Dutch pink and English pink are also described as having a greenish yellow tone [11]. The books call the reason a yellow lake was called "pink" unexplained, and a German-verb origin is only speculation [11].

Paterson's dictionary files the shade under many names, among them [[lime-yellow]], linden green, tarragon, acacia and the learned *luteo-virescent*, and he calls [[cadmium-lemon]] a bright greenish yellow [12]. Quinoline yellow, a food additive coded E104, is described as a greenish yellow [12].

sections.title: Khaki, mustard and a disliked color
sections.body:
Pastoureau remarks in a note that mustard and greenish yellow still strike European viewers as the least agreeable shades, citing his own 1992 dictionary of modern colors [13]. The modern world nevertheless put them to use. Pastoureau notes that modern clothing added some deliberately unlovely greens, chosen because they last, hide stains and let a wearer blend into the landscape. They went into uniforms for dirty trades and for armies, and they sit in a mustard or greenish-yellow range [14].

The best-known is [[khaki]], which does not come from the French name of the persimmon but from a Hindustani word meaning earth or dust color [14]. British soldiers of the Indian armies were the first to wear it, in the second half of the nineteenth century, and other Western armies soon followed [14]. Another leaf-and-earth tone close by is [[mustard]].

sections.title: How the eye separates it from yellow
sections.body:
Greenish yellow is a narrow place on the spectrum with a wide effect on the eye. Light of 580 nanometers looks greenish yellow, but light of 585 looks plain yellow, a difference of about one per cent in wavelength that is enough to change the color name [15]. Eckstut and her co-author point out that people distinguish many changes between 580 and 585 nanometers, whereas blues between 420 and 440 all look alike [16]. They also use it to show opponent colors: we can picture a greenish yellow, but not a red-green or a blue-yellow [16].

An older book adds a claim of its own. Birren (1950) quotes Ferree and Rand that the clearest and fastest seeing comes from the yellow, orange-yellow and greenish-yellow region of the spectrum, which is old opinion rather than modern evidence [17].

Gurney gives a way to see the color for yourself: in a demonstration with colored croquet balls, the reflected light of a green ball pushed the shadow of a yellow ball toward greenish yellow, while a red ball pushed it toward orange [18]. Look in the shadow beside a yellow object and you can find it.

sections.title: In painting
sections.body: Gage observes that yellow and green had rarely been clearly separated since Antiquity, and that Mondrian, in a number of paintings, used a distinctly greenish yellow or an apple green as his third primary, as if to reconcile Ostwald's primary yellow with green [19]. The small flower of the madder plant, famous for its red root, is itself described as greenish yellow [20]. In our archive the painter who reaches for it most is [[painter:pierre-bonnard|Bonnard]] [21].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 163 contain this color within six units of ΔE over at least five per cent of the canvas, or 0.7 per cent [21]. It is mostly an accent: in 87 per cent of the paintings where it appears, it is among the lightest colors, not a mid-tone [21].

The largest concentrations are not European oils [21]. The Kalighat school of Bengal, a style of popular paintings, carries it in 31 of 96 works, 47 times the archive rate, and India as a whole in 37 of 721, 7.5 times the rate [21]. The photographs are of aged paper and varnish, which drift toward this hue, so part of that lift may be the age of the object and not the pigment [21]. Among painters, Bonnard has it in 5 of his 45 paintings, 16 times the rate, and Gauguin in 3 of 50 [21]. By decade it peaks in the 1890s, in 44 of 1,173 paintings, or 3.8 per cent [21].

In printed English, "greenish yellow" peaks around 1857, and by 2000 it is about a fifth as common as at its peak (Google Books, all senses of the words) [22]. Against white, the swatch has a contrast ratio of only 2.1, so text in this color on a white page is hard to read; against black it is 9.8 [1]. All archive numbers are as photographed; a color match is not a pigment test.

openers: Light of 580 nanometers is greenish yellow; 585 is yellow, and that one per cent is enough to change the name.
Rome had a rare word for a disliked yellow, and scholars still argue about whether it meant greenish.
